Windows Event Logs: An event log is a timeline generated by Windows providers. A channel groups related events, while the event ID describes the event type for a given provider. Interpret the result with identity, logon type, host, and timestamp.
A successful service logon differs from an interactive sign-in even when both share event 4624.
Authentication auditing makes account activity visible and helps analysts separate evidence from assumptions.
Linux Logs: The system journal stores messages from services and applications. A unit identifies a supervised service. Read the timestamp, program, identity, and operation before linking two records.
An sshd message can describe a login while a sudo message describes a separate privilege decision.
Administrators need an attributable timeline when names, clocks, and log retention differ.
Networking: Communication depends on addressing, routing, transport, and an application protocol. A prefix describes a network, a port identifies a service endpoint, and an observation point determines which part of a flow is visible.
A host can route to a subnet while one application connection still fails. A route and an open service are different observations.
Troubleshooting the right layer avoids treating a resolution, transport, or application problem as the same failure.
Wireshark: A packet capture is a record of frames visible at a selected interface. Display filters choose which captured records you inspect. Header fields can support a conclusion even when application payloads are encrypted.
A captured SYN without a reply proves that one SYN was observed. Capture position and duration limit conclusions about missing responses.
Traffic analysis depends on timestamps, flow identifiers, and a clear statement of what the capture cannot prove.
Linux: Linux processes run under a user and one or more groups. A filesystem path points to an object whose permissions limit access. Local listeners, configuration, and journal messages describe different aspects of system behavior.
A report in a private directory can have separate permissions from a redacted copy in a shared directory.
Read-only inventories and least privilege help a defender verify configuration while preserving system state.
SIEM: A security information and event management system collects and normalizes multiple event sources. A detection queries the normalized records. An alert is a rule result that still needs interpretation and corroboration.
A quiet dashboard can mean expected activity, a collection outage, or a field mismatch in a query.
An analysis is only as complete as its telemetry coverage, time window, and field definitions.
Wazuh: Wazuh can collect endpoint events through agents, interpret them with decoders, and apply detection rules. The dashboard shows indexed results. Verify each stage before explaining missing alerts.
An agent heartbeat demonstrates connectivity. It does not prove an event was collected, decoded, or indexed.
Tracing the pipeline helps find evidence gaps without prematurely tuning detection thresholds.
Detection Engineering: A detection converts an observable behavior into a condition over fields, groups, and time. Positive, benign, and missing-field test cases show what the condition can and cannot distinguish.
Repeated authentication failures can match a threshold rule even during a planned system change.
Testing detections against realistic controls helps analysts manage false positives and audit coverage.
Threat Hunting: A hunt starts with a testable hypothesis about observable behavior. Compare it with a baseline, seek independent evidence, and record what would disprove the hypothesis.
An unexpected program might be explained by a maintenance ticket and matching installation logs.
A bounded question reduces false attribution and makes future hunts reproducible.
Incident Investigation: An investigation preserves source records, normalizes time, and builds a timeline of observations. Separate confirmed facts, assumptions, and missing evidence. Correlation alone does not prove causation.
A router and an endpoint may show different times for the same connection because their clocks differ.
Evidence quality affects escalation and determines what a reviewer can reproduce.
Incident Response: Incident response includes preparation, assessment, containment, recovery, and review. The right action depends on authority, evidence, system impact, and recovery criteria.
A suspicious login can justify collecting logs while a confirmed account compromise can justify authorized containment.
Unplanned changes can destroy evidence or interrupt legitimate service, so document decisions and approval.
Enumeration: Enumeration inventories systems and services in an explicitly permitted scope. An observed endpoint, a service label, and a verified product version are separate claims. Read results together with the vantage point and boundaries.
A recorded 443/tcp listener indicates reachability from the original observation point. The port number does not guarantee HTTPS or the absence of a weakness.
Accurate inventories prevent unsupported findings and keep assessment work within authorization.
Nmap: Nmap inventory reports represent observations from a particular collector and time. An open, closed, or filtered state describes the available response. Banners and inferred labels require corroboration.
A filtered result cannot tell you for certain whether the service is open or closed.
Interpreting saved inventories carefully keeps reachability, identification, and vulnerability claims separate.
Burp Suite: An HTTP inspection tool displays request and response records. A request has a method, headers, and possibly a body. A response exposes a status and returned data, but does not reveal every server-side decision.
In a redacted export, two responses can show different account identifiers without proving how access was checked internally.
Evidence review supports secure design and fixes while protecting session data and respecting scope.
Web Security: Web applications cross trust boundaries between the client, server, and backend resources. Authentication identifies a user. Authorization decides which actions or records are allowed. Validation protects how input is interpreted.
A successful sign-in does not automatically authorize the user to read every tenant's resources.
Separating identity, policy, and input checks helps a reviewer recommend an appropriate defensive change.
Vulnerability Assessment: A vulnerability is a weakness under specified conditions. An advisory, inventory match, and verified configuration evidence represent different confidence levels. Exposure and business impact help set remediation priorities.
The same missing patch can have a different priority on an isolated lab VM and an exposed critical service.
A defensible report explains the evidence, context, remediation owner, and safe verification criteria.
Pentesting Reports: An assessment report lists scope, observation, evidence limits, impact, and recommended remediation. A verification criterion describes a safe check that confirms the fix. Remove private identifiers from shared examples.
An observed configuration gap can be documented without claiming that an attacker exploited it.
A clear report lets another person verify the observation and prioritize remediation without repeating unsafe actions.
Python Automation: Automation applies a repeatable rule to structured input. Validate fields, handle malformed rows, and state the counting unit. A synthetic fixture makes expected behavior auditable.
Three event rows can describe one repeated incident or identity. A summary should distinguish row counts and unique subjects.
Tests with known inputs catch parsing errors and make evidence transformations reproducible.
